title: Patanjali 1.1–1.16: "now, yoga"; yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings; practice and non-attachment (7 of 7)
hook: letting go of what you've seen, and of what you've only heard about, and then a letting go beyond that
tomorrow: the lineage tracks begin: karma, bhakti, jnana

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patanjali 1.14: a long time, without break, with care, and practice becomes firm ground. Three hundred days. Your line: now. Today, the other wing, and the week closes. Day three hundred one.

Some things pull at you because you've tasted them. The last slice of cake. The ping of a new message. The feeling of being right in an argument. And some things pull at you because you've only heard about them. The trip everyone posts about. The life your cousin seems to have. The perfect calm that serious meditators supposedly reach. Patanjali noticed both kinds of pull, and he named them in the same breath. Then, in the very next thread, he went one step further.
screen: `WHAT YOU'VE TASTED.` → `WHAT YOU'VE ONLY HEARD ABOUT.` → `ONE STEP FURTHER.`

segments.voice: Thread fifteen: non-attachment is the mastery of one who no longer thirsts for things seen, or things heard about. Seen means this world: the cake, the praise, the paycheck. Heard about means everything promised by tradition or rumor, and the old commentators include heavenly rewards here too. Even spiritual prizes can become one more thing to crave. The word Patanjali uses for the result is vashikara: mastery, being in charge of the pull rather than pulled by it. Notice he doesn't say the cake disappears. You can still eat the cake. It just doesn't own you. Then thread sixteen, the higher kind: from knowing the seer, the purusha, comes freedom from thirst even for the gunas, the basic strands that make up everything in nature. That's a letting go at the root. Not just of this craving or that one, but of the whole weave, because you've seen what you are underneath it. Now look back at the whole week. Thread one: now. Thread two: yoga is the stilling of the mind's turnings. Three and four: the seer resting in itself, or looking like its thoughts, a crystal beside a red flower. Five to eleven: the five turnings, sleep among them. Twelve: two wings, practice and letting go. Thirteen and fourteen: the long, steady, careful practice that becomes firm ground. And today, fifteen and sixteen: letting go of what you've tasted and what you've heard of, and at last, of the thirst itself. Sixteen threads. One week. And it all started with one word: now.
screen: `NO THIRST FOR THINGS SEEN OR HEARD OF.` · `VASHIKARA: MASTERY OF THE PULL.` · `THE HIGHER KIND: FREE AT THE ROOT.` · `SIXTEEN THREADS, ONE WEEK.` · then, large: `TAT PARAṀ PURUṢA-KHYĀTER GUṆA-VAITṚṢṆYAM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let one pull come to mind. Something you've tasted and want again, or something you've only heard about and want anyway. Hold it gently. Notice where you feel it: the chest, the stomach, the hands. Breathe into that place. You don't have to give the thing up. Just loosen your grip on it by one finger, then another. Stay with the wanting, and notice that it doesn't have to own you. If you pray, you can offer the wanting to God. The bell holds the time.
Patanjali 1.1, and all sixteen threads to 1.16: now, the stilling of the turnings, practice and letting go, all the way down to the root.
Your line: now. Today, when something pulls at you, enjoy it or don't, but loosen your grip by one finger. Now. Day three hundred one.

screen: `DAY 301 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE TRACKS BEGIN — KARMA, BHAKTI, JNANA.`

howItsDone: In Hindu teaching, vairagya is not only for monks: householders are taught to hold wealth, family and even religious rewards loosely, and the Yoga Sutras' opening chapter is often studied as a complete short course in meditation.

fork.setup: you've heard that serious meditators reach perfect calm, and you want it badly. what would thread fifteen say about that wanting?
options: it's one more pull, a thing heard about.
keep craving until you get it.
fork.reveal: thread fifteen names things seen and things heard of. even spiritual prizes can become one more thing to crave.

original.note: Sanskrit: non-attachment, dispassion; from vi + raga, without coloring or passion.

trapdoor: what you thought: non-attachment means not caring.
what it means: no longer thirsting for things seen or heard of, and at last, freedom at the root.
what a scholar hears: anushravika, 'heard of', traditionally covers rewards promised by scripture, like heaven; 1.16's para-vairagya rests on purusha-khyati, discerning the seer.

notes: Week 43 closes here with a look-back over sutras 1.1–1.16.
Anushravika 'heard of' as including scriptural promises (e.g. heaven) follows the classical commentary; confirm.
Gunas summarized as 'the basic strands that make up everything in nature' (sattva, rajas, tamas); confirm.
The close teases the lineage tracks (302–322). The index title for 302 lists all three tracks; see the note on day 302 about how these scripts handle the track choice.
